title: Crystal Lattices and Solid State Physics
short_intro: A crystal lattice is a three-dimensional periodic array of points representing the positions of atoms, ions, or molecules in a crystalline solid. It provides the foundational framework for analyzing the structural, thermal, and electronic properties of solids through periodicity and translational symmetry.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Basic definition of space lattice, basis, unit cell, types of crystal systems, Bravais lattices, and Bragg's Law of X-ray diffraction.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Reciprocal lattice vectors, Brillouin zones, atomic packing factor calculations, crystal binding energy, and Miller indices calculations for planes and directions.

concept_notes.heading: Crystal Lattice and Basis
bullets: A space lattice is an infinite array of discrete points in three dimensions where each point has an identical environment.
A crystal structure is formed by attaching a motif or basis of one or more atoms to every lattice point: Crystal Structure = Lattice + Basis.

Translational symmetry of the lattice is defined by the translation vector R = n<sub>1</sub>a + n<sub>2</sub>b + n<sub>3</sub>c, where a, b, c are primitive translation vectors and n<sub>i</sub> are integers.

concept_notes.heading: Unit Cell and Bravais Lattices
bullets: A unit cell is the fundamental geometric block that, when repeated in three dimensions, generates the entire crystal lattice.
Primitive unit cell contains only one lattice point and possesses the minimum volume.
There are 7 crystal systems (cubic, tetragonal, orthorhombic, monoclinic, triclinic, hexagonal, rhombohedral) which expand into 14 Bravais lattices in three dimensions.

concept_notes.heading: Miller Indices and Interplanar Spacing
bullets: Miller indices (hkl) are a set of integers used to designate crystallographic planes, obtained by taking the reciprocals of fractional intercepts the plane makes with the crystal axes, cleared of fractions.
The interplanar spacing d<sub>hkl</sub> depends on the Miller indices and the lattice parameters.
For a cubic system with lattice parameter a, the interplanar spacing is given by d<sub>hkl</sub> = a / sqrt(h<sup>2</sup> + k<sup>2</sup> + l<sup>2</sup>).

concept_notes.heading: Reciprocal Lattice
bullets: The reciprocal lattice is a lattice in Fourier space corresponding to the direct crystal lattice, crucial for analyzing diffraction and band structures.
The primitive reciprocal vectors are defined as a* = 2\pi (b \times c) / (a \cdot (b \times c)), with cyclic permutations.
The volume of a reciprocal unit cell is inversely proportional to the volume of the direct real-space unit cell.

derivations.title: Bragg's Law of X-ray Diffraction
derivations.conditions: Monochromatic X-rays incident on parallel crystal planes with spacing d at grazing angle \theta.
steps: Consider two parallel atomic planes separated by an interplanar distance d.
X-ray waves strike the planes at an angle \theta. The path difference between rays reflected from successive planes is derived from geometry as \Delta = d \sin\theta + d \sin\theta = 2d \sin\theta.
For constructive interference to occur, the path difference must be an integral multiple of the wavelength \lambda.

derivations.title: Interplanar Spacing for Cubic Crystal System
derivations.conditions: Cubic crystal system with lattice parameter a and Miller indices (hkl).
steps: Consider a plane (hkl) making intercepts a/h, a/k, and a/l along the three orthogonal axes x, y, and z.
The normal unit vector n to the plane has direction cosines proportional to (h/a, k/a, l/a).
The interplanar spacing d is the perpendicular distance from the origin to the plane, expressed as d = (a/h) \cos\alpha = a / \sqrt{h^2 + k^2 + l^2}.

graphs_and_experiments.title: X-ray Diffractometer Intensity vs 2\theta Graph
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Sharp intensity peaks plotted against scattering angle 2\theta representing distinct crystallographic planes.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Each peak corresponds to a specific set of Miller indices (hkl) satisfying Bragg's law, confirming crystal structure and lattice spacing.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Used to identify crystal structures (SC, BCC, FCC) via systematic absences.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Simple Cubic, BCC, and FCC Unit Cell Geometry
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Cubic outlines with corner atoms (SC), body-centered atom (BCC), and face-centered atoms (FCC).
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Visualizes coordination number (6 for SC, 8 for BCC, 12 for FCC) and packing efficiency.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Direct questions on effective atoms per unit cell and atomic packing factor.

graphs_and_experiments.title: First Brillouin Zone in 1D
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A line segment from -\pi/a to \pi/a representing wave vector k space.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Represents the first region of wave vectors where electron waves undergo Bragg reflection from the periodic lattice.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Understanding energy band gaps in solid-state physics.

solved_numericals.question: Calculate the interplanar spacing for (110) planes in a simple cubic lattice having a lattice parameter of 0.3 nm.
solution_steps: Identify given parameters: a = 0.3 nm, h = 1, k = 1, l = 0.
Use the interplanar spacing formula for a cubic system: d = a / \sqrt{h^2 + k^2 + l^2}.
Calculate final numerical value: d = 0.3 / 1.414 = 0.212 nm.

solved_numericals.question: X-rays of wavelength 0.154 nm are diffracted from (111) planes of a face-centered cubic crystal with lattice parameter 0.4 nm at first-order diffraction. Find the Bragg angle.
solution_steps: Find interplanar spacing d for (111) in cubic system: d = a / \sqrt{1^2 + 1^2 + 1^2} = 0.4 / \sqrt{3} nm = 0.2309 nm.
Apply Bragg's law: 2d \sin\theta = n\lambda with n = 1.

solved_numericals.question: Determine the atomic packing factor for a Body-Centered Cubic (BCC) crystal structure assuming hard sphere contact along the body diagonal.
solution_steps: Relation between lattice parameter a and atomic radius r for BCC: 4r = \sqrt{3}a, hence a = 4r / \sqrt{3}.
Number of atoms per unit cell for BCC, Z = 2.
Volume of unit cell V_c = a^3 = (4r / \sqrt{3})^3 = 64r^3 / (3\sqrt{3}).
Total volume of spheres in unit cell V_s = 2 \times (4/3)\pi r^3 = (8/3)\pi r^3.

assumptions_and_limitations: Crystals are assumed to be infinitely periodic, ignoring finite size effects and surface boundaries.
Thermal vibrations of atoms are initially neglected in static geometrical lattice models (harmonic approximation used later).
Real crystals contain point defects, dislocations, and impurities which break exact periodicity.

common_misconceptions.wrong: A crystal lattice and crystal structure are identical physical entities.
common_misconceptions.correct: A crystal lattice is purely a mathematical array of points, whereas crystal structure is lattice plus basis.
common_misconceptions.why: The lattice provides only the periodicity; the basis determines the actual atoms placed at each lattice point.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Miller indices (hkl) represent a single unique lattice point.
common_misconceptions.correct: Miller indices represent a family of parallel crystallographic planes throughout the crystal.
common_misconceptions.why: Planes with the same ratio of intercepts define parallel planes having identical interplanar spacing.

quick_revision: There are 7 crystal systems and 14 Bravais lattices.
Cubic interplanar spacing: d_{hkl} = a / \sqrt{h^2 + k^2 + l^2}
